title: Why Wasoko's Founder Chose a Merger of Equals With Egypt's MaxAB
dek: Daniel Yu built a Nairobi network that supplied kiosks by text message, then merged it with an Egyptian rival and shared the top job.

story.event: Merging Wasoko with Egypt's MaxAB after years supplying informal shops by phone order
story.summary: Daniel Yu's Sokowatch, later Wasoko, let informal shopkeepers in Nairobi order stock by text message for free delivery and grew across East Africa on venture funding. In December 2023 it agreed a merger of equals with Egypt's MaxAB; overlapping jobs were cut and Wasoko left Zambia, Uganda and Zanzibar before the all-stock deal closed in August 2024 with Yu and Belal El-Megharbel as co-chief executives. Yu stepped out of his full-time role in September 2025.
paragraphs: Around 2017, a shopkeeper in Nairobi could send a text message ordering maize flour, soap or cooking oil and have it delivered to the kiosk free, instead of closing up to travel to a wholesaler. That was Sokowatch, started by Daniel Yu, a Californian who had left the University of Chicago. He said the idea grew from months studying Arabic in Egypt, where he saw shops short of goods and mobile phones everywhere. A first version for health clinics, Relief Watch, raised $600,000 before he concluded it would not work and turned to consumer goods. By May 2017 Sokowatch supplied more than 5,000 Nairobi shops.

It grew on investors' money. Renamed Wasoko, it raised $125 million in 2022 at a valuation of $625 million, in a round led by Tiger Global and Avenir. In December 2023 Wasoko and MaxAB, an Egyptian company doing similar work for small shops in North Africa, announced preliminary terms for what they called a merger of equals. Their statement said Wasoko's monthly revenue had risen 30% that year and that the deal brought new investment and runway to reach profitability. Yu tied it to his own beginnings, "reflecting my personal history developing the initial concept behind Wasoko during my time spent in Egypt over a decade ago."

Joining meant giving things up. In January 2024 TechCabal reported that the two companies, with about 4,000 staff between them, would cut roughly a tenth of that workforce; one person said they were told on a video call that MaxAB's Egyptian team would take over product and engineering. Yu confirmed that those affected had been offered severance "in line with local laws" and could keep their stock options. In March 2024 Wasoko closed in Zambia, Uganda and Zanzibar.

The deal closed in August 2024, four months later than planned, as an all-stock merger with a shareholding Yu described as "pretty close to 50-50." He and MaxAB's co-founder Belal El-Megharbel became co-chief executives of a Cairo-headquartered company in five countries, claiming 450,000 merchants. About a year later, in September 2025, Yu stepped out of his full-time role to become an adviser, and El-Megharbel became sole chief executive.

quote.text: There must be very two, before there can be very one. Let it be an alliance of two large, formidable natures, mutually beheld, mutually feared, before yet they recognize the deep identity which, beneath these disparities, unites them.
quote.source_title: Essays — First Series, Project Gutenberg eBook #2944
quote.connection: Emerson held that a true alliance needs two strong parties before it can become one. Wasoko and MaxAB began as near-equals with two chief executives, and a year later had one. Whether that was the alliance maturing or one side giving way, the record does not say.

reflection: A merger is rarely the ending a founder imagines at the start. Yu had spent years building a company from his own idea, and he agreed to share it, to cut roles that overlapped and to close markets he had opened. The statements spoke of runway and scale; the people on that video call heard something harder.

Some of your choices will also mean giving up a little control so the work survives: sharing a project, or letting a colleague's way of doing things replace yours. It is fair to mourn what you give up and still choose it. It is also fair to ask, before agreeing, what being equals will mean in a year.
invitation: Think of one piece of work you share with someone. Write a sentence on what each of you decides alone and what you decide together, then ask them this week whether they would write it the same way.

research_notes: Founding date: sources disagree (2013 in Wamda, Disrupt Africa and WeeTracker; 2014 in TechMoran; 2015 in MENAbytes); Yu's own statement in the December 2023 announcement says he launched Wasoko in Kenya in 2016. The story avoids a founding year and dates the Nairobi model by the May 2017 Disrupt Africa interview. Layoffs: TechCabal (January 2024) reported a cut of roughly 10% of a combined workforce of about 4,000; TechCabal (August 2024) said Wasoko made 100 duplicated roles redundant in December 2023. These may describe different counts or stages, so the story gives the January report with its attribution and no single Wasoko figure. Market exits: TechCabal names Zambia, Uganda and Zanzibar (March 2024); WeeTracker lists Uganda, Zambia and Senegal plus the Zanzibar office; the story uses TechCabal's list. Funding: TechCabal cites Crunchbase for $143.6 million raised by Wasoko alone; MENAbytes and TechCabal give over $230 million for both companies together; WeeTracker attributes $230 million to Wasoko, which appears to be the combined figure; the story gives only the 2022 round. WeeTracker reports that investor VNV Global marked Wasoko down to $260 million in early 2024; this is after the December 2023 decision and is not used in the story. The 450,000 merchants and 30% revenue growth are company claims and are presented as such. The Relief Watch pivot and $600,000 figure come from the 2018 podcast's episode notes summarising Yu's account. The TechCrunch interview of August 2024 could not be loaded; Yu's '50-50' remark is cited from TechCabal, which reports he told it the same on a call. Yu's relocation and personal reasons for stepping back are left out for privacy. Emerson is writing about friendship between two people; the passage is applied to a merger by analogy.
